hypothesis_mapping.claim: Engineered interlayer twist angles designed to suppress cross-plane thermal conductivity in van der Waals heterostructures remain structurally stable under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients, provided the interlayer binding energy exceeds a critical threshold determined by the twist-angle-dependent moiré potential landscape, and in the absence of confounding defect-mediated or chemically-induced interlayer pinning.
hypothesis_mapping.decision_rule: Structural stability is accepted if the twist angle, measured after thermal cycling, remains within the pre-cycling uncertainty interval and the cross-plane thermal conductivity retention exceeds the pre-specified threshold.

outcome_branches.conclusion_scope: The structural stability of the engineered twist angles fails when the interlayer binding energy falls below the critical threshold determined by the local moiré potential energy barriers, or when defect-mediated pinning and interlayer chemical bonding become the dominant retention mechanisms, masking the true moiré potential threshold.

alternative_explanations: Thermal cycling induces interlayer diffusion or chemical bonding that pins the layers independently of the moiré potential.
Changes in thermal contact resistance during cycling mimic changes in intrinsic cross-plane thermal conductivity.

Defect-mediated interlayer pinning (e.g., via chalcogen vacancies) or thermally induced chemical bonding could maintain suppressed cross-plane thermal conductivity, mimicking the effect of moiré potential energy barriers.
Strain relaxation via wrinkle formation or localized delamination could alter thermal transport without actual twist-angle relaxation.
assumptions: Interlayer binding energy and moiré potential depths can be accurately calculated or measured for diverse van der Waals material families.
Thermal cycling conditions can be selected to minimize interlayer diffusion and chemical bonding, ensuring moiré potential pinning is the dominant retention mechanism.
boundary_conditions: The structural stability of the engineered twist angles fails when the interlayer binding energy falls below the critical threshold determined by the local moiré potential energy barriers, or when defect-mediated pinning and interlayer chemical bonding become the dominant retention mechanisms, masking the true moiré potential threshold.
reasoning_context.claim_scope: The structural stability of twist-angle-engineered thermal anisotropy in van der Waals heterostructures under operational thermal cycling, bounded by the moiré potential landscape in regimes free from defect-mediated or chemically-induced interlayer pinning.
falsifiers: Demonstration that engineered twist angles relax to equilibrium stacking within device-relevant thermal cycling conditions in the absence of defect-mediated or chemical pinning, resulting in recovery of cross-plane conductivity to within 20% of pristine aligned values.

gap_records.statement: The extreme thermal anisotropy mechanism is validated only for MoS2 and WS2, leaving its applicability to other van der Waals materials unverified.
gap_records.why_it_matters: The abstract explicitly reports measurements and molecular dynamics simulations exclusively for MoS2 and WS2, without addressing whether random interlayer rotations yield similar anisotropy ratios in materials with different phonon dispersion or interlayer bonding characteristics.

gap_records.statement: The persistence of random interlayer rotations under sustained thermal cycling and operational stress gradients is unaddressed.
gap_records.why_it_matters: While the abstract establishes interlayer rotation as a design degree of freedom for directed heat transport, it does not discuss whether these rotational configurations remain stable or relax over time when subjected to the very thermal gradients they are engineered to mitigate.

operational_definitions: A heterostructure sample is operationally defined as a stack of two or more 2D layers transferred to a designated substrate with a target twist angle set during assembly.
Thermal cycling is operationally defined as a repeated sequence of controlled temperature excursions and returns within a declared range and number of cycles.
Twist-angle retention is operationally defined as the difference between the nominal assembly angle and the angle measured on the same region of the sample after a defined cycling interval.
